title: Beyond the Batch: Momentum-Updated Virtual Cohorts for 3D PET-CT Prognosis
reviewer_1_strengths: Addresses a practically important bottleneck: The paper tackles a real limitation of 3D medical survival modeling, namely the mismatch between memory-intensive full-field-of-view 3D imaging and the large effective risk sets preferred by survival objectives. The proposed framework offers a reasonable way to alleviate this issue without relying on aggressive cropping or downsampling that may discard clinically relevant context. Reasonably general framework: The proposed Momentum Contrast Survival Framework (MCSF) appears to be reasonably model-agnostic and can be integrated with multiple common 3D backbones for end-to-end learning. The ablation experiments suggest that the gains are not restricted to a single encoder design. Thoughtful treatment of historical features: The use of an evolving reference encoder is a sensible design choice for mitigating the instability that may arise when reusing historical representations. In addition, the time-aware weighting mechanism is well motivated and helps reduce the influence of ambiguous pairwise comparisons. Consistent empirical improvements: The reported results on two distinct cancer cohorts are encouraging and suggest that the method can improve survival prediction performance over the included baselines. The Kaplan-Meier stratification results further support the practical utility of the approach.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The model’s input pre-processing stage relies on a binarised lesion segmentation mask as a spatial prior, applying affine transformations and reweighting to the PET and CT channels. As the datasets used in the experiments all contain pre-existing segmentation masks, this implies that, for practical clinical deployment, the framework must be paired with a high-precision automatic segmentation model or rely on manual annotation. 2.This paper suffers from shortcomings in terms of experimental rigour and persuasiveness; it lacks quantitative data such as the number of parameters, FLOPs and GPU memory usage. This not only contradicts its central claim of ‘resolving computational bottlenecks’, but also fails to provide quantitative evidence to account for the additional computational overhead incurred by training two networks in parallel. 3.The empirical comparison remains somewhat limited, as the main baselines are predominantly generic 3D CNN backbones and an NLL variant, while direct comparisons against stronger survival-specific models are missing. This makes it difficult to isolate whether the gains come primarily from the proposed survival formulation or from favorable backbone/task settings.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper tackles a relevant practical issue: in 3D PET-CT survival modeling, small mini-batches can make Cox-style risk-set estimation unstable. The proposed virtual cohort bank is intuitive and fits the application setting well. The time-aware weighting is a reasonable way to reduce ambiguous comparisons. Results on two cohorts are promising, and the ablation suggests both VCB and TAPRL contribute.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat limited from the current presentation. The method appears to combine momentum encoder, memory bank, and pairwise ranking ideas in a survival setting, but the distinction from related momentum-contrastive / ranking-based work is not yet very clear. The role of the lesion mask prior is unclear. The method uses mask-guided input modulation, but I could not tell whether all baselines received the same mask information, or whether this component was ablated separately. This makes attribution of the gains harder. The need for full-volume training is asserted rather than fully justified. It would help if the paper clarified why ROI/crop-based alternatives are not appropriate in this setting. Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation details of the queue: what exactly is stored, whether queued scores/features are refreshed, and whether both event and censored samples are enqueued. The computational tradeoff is not discussed. Since the method adds a reference encoder and a virtual bank, some comment on runtime/memory overhead would help.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The mismatch between the global nature of Cox partial likelihood and the severely constrained batch sizes in 3D medical imaging is a genuine and under-addressed issue. 2.able 2 evaluates VCB and TAPRL separately across three backbones on both datasets, showing consistent additive gains. Table 3 examines VCB size sensitivity, including the non-monotonic degradation at K=128, which is an honest and informative result. 3.Using lesion masks as a learnable spatial prior for PET/CT weighting is a sensible way to focus the backbone on relevant regions without hard masking.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The larger and more impactful dataset (1,210 patients) is from a private collection. No dataset characteristics (cancer subtype, staging, treatment, event rate, follow-up duration) are reported. This makes reproducibility and generalizability of the main results unverifiable. 2.TAPRL combines (a) enlarging the risk pool via VCB and (b) time-aware weighting. Table 2 ablates VCB vs VCB+TAPRL but does not separately evaluate the time-aware weighting against a flat-weighted version of the enlarged risk set. It is therefore unclear whether the temporal weighting provides benefit beyond simply having a larger risk pool. 3.The paper compares only against backbone architectures trained with Cox or NLL loss on the in-batch risk set. There is no comparison against other large-risk-set Cox approximations. This significantly limits the positioning of MCSF relative to prior work. The momentum encoder is justified by analogy to MoCo, but the degree of feature drift in the VCB and its impact on risk score consistency across iterations is never analyzed. 5.Panels d and e (ResNet34 and SEResNeXt50) show p > 0.05 for log-rank tests, which is presented without comment. The comparison between methods via KM significance is not a reliable metric for model comparison, and framing it as evidence of superiority is misleading.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers(R) and have responded with the necessary information. Q1: Computational cost.(R1R2) A1: Taking ResNet-18 as an baseline, MCSF increased parameters from 8.3M to 16.6M, forward FLOPs from 285G to 570G, and GPU memory from 6036M to 7686M. The reference encoder is EMA-updated without gradient backpropagation, limiting additional training overhead. Inference uses only the main encoder, cost equals baseline. Q2: Mask and ROI.(AC,R1R2) A2: All compared models used the same mask-guided input modulation, ensuring fair comparison. Full-volume training was adopted because PET-CT lesions are spatially sparse and may include metastatic lymph nodes and even occult metastasis; ROI cropping may miss clinically relevant disease. Internal masks were generated by our in-house segmentation model and clinically reviewed. Missing H&N masks were inferred using the open-source weights of the 2025 H&N challenge winner. We will release our segmentation weights. Q3: Baseline Selection and Survival Models.(R1R4) A3: ResNet with Cox or NLL losses remains a mainstream paradigm for 3D medical prognosis. We focused on the risk-set bottleneck within this standard framework to isolate MCSF’s contribution. Consistent gains over these established baselines support our framework’s efficacy. Q4: Novelty.(AC,R2)： A4: To the best of our knowledge, MCSF is the first framework to integrate momentum-based memory mechanisms with survival theory to address the small-batch bottleneck in 3D imaging. Unlike conventional momentum-contrastive methods that store features for instance discrimination, MCSF stores risk scores, event times, and labels to approximate a global virtual cohort. This enables each event sample to be ranked beyond the local mini-batch. TAPRL further leverages temporal separation to reduce noisy pairs, making the framework specifically tailored to survival analysis rather than a simple combination of existing methods. Q5: Details for queue.(AC,R2) A5: The queue stores risk scores, event times, and labels. After each batch, the latest patients are enqueued and the oldest samples are removed. Both event and censored patients are enqueued. Existing queued scores are not re-computed; their consistency is maintained by the EMA encoder. Q6: Private Dataset.(AC,R4) A6: The private cohort included I–III stage patients. The maximum follow-up time was 13 years; the event rate was 9.8%. The data includes all subtypes, and treatments include surgery and neoadjuvant therapy. Q7: Ablation for TAPRL.(R4) A7: TAPRL was designed as a refinement of VCB rather than an independent module: VCB restores sufficient cross-patient comparisons under small-batch 3D training, while TAPRL reduces noise by down-weighting temporally ambiguous pairs. Currently, we justify this design theoretically, and a flat-weighted VCB ranking ablation will be included in future work. Q8: Other large-risk-set Cox approximations.(AC,R4) A8: Existing methods mainly target low-dimensional features, where historical samples can be revisited. This is impractical for 3D PET-CT due to memory constraints. MCSF instead stores EMA-derived scores, enlarging the risk set without backpropagating historical 3D volumes. Q9: Feature drift.(R4) A9: The EMA encoder aims to smooth parameter updates and maintain more consistent stored risk scores. Table3 indirectly suggests the potential impact of feature drift: performance drops when increasing VCB from K=64 to 128, likely due to older representations. We will clarify this rationale in the revision. Q10: KM interpretation.(R4) A10: We agree that KM analysis is related to risk discrimination but does not strictly correspond to C-index. In the revision, we will explicitly note that panels d and e show non-significant log-rank results, indicating limited separation for these two baseline models, and present KM curves only as supportive qualitative evidence of risk stratification. These essential details will be clarified in the revision.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Although two reviewers gave an accept rating, one reviewer leaned negative due to insufficient separation of the framework’s contribution from the lesion-mask prior, underspecified methodological details, and unclear novelty relative to existing memory-bank or ranking-based approaches. They also mentioned weaknesses, including an inadequately characterized private dataset and a lack of comparison with existing Cox approximation methods. The authors should clearly defend their paper against these issues. | The authors have adequately addressed all of the reviewers’ concerns. Accordingly, I recommend acceptance of the paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have clarified several of the reviewers’ concerns, notably the computational overhead and experimental protocol. Despite the remaining shortcomings, there is a consensus for acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers unanimously provided positive recommendations, and I agree with their decision.

title: CT-Conditioned Diffusion Prior with Physics-Constrained Sampling for PET Super-Resolution
reviewer_1_strengths: The problem is well-motivated and relevant, as PET super-resolution is inherently ill-posed and depends on scanner-specific physics. The use of CT as conditioning is practical and clinically accessible, providing useful anatomical guidance. The framework combines diffusion priors with physics-based constraints, which is aligned with current best practices in inverse problems. The paper includes comparisons with multiple state-of-the-art methods, covering both supervised and diffusion-based approaches. The method demonstrates consistent improvements in both standard and OOD settings, as well as lesion-level evaluation, which strengthens its empirical impact.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Some implementation details are not sufficiently described, which may limit reproducibility. The evaluation is based on simulated degradations and 2D slice-wise experiments, which may not fully reflect real-world clinical scenarios. Certain claims (e. g. , hallucination reduction) are not directly supported by dedicated evaluation.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper uses high-quality CT image as a guide for PET reconstruction, and apply cross-attention for CT and PET. This method may improve the anatomical results for PET reconstruction. 2.It incorporates comprehensive physics constraints in reconstruction, including PSF modeling and Progressive Physics-Constrained Refinement, which improves the final reconstruction quality via ablation study.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper compares its results with some previous diffusion model based reconstruction methods (such as ScorePET), but it didn’t make a clear comparison on how the proposed method is different from previous diffusion reconstruction methods.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper proposes a diffusion sampler for PET resolution enhancement. The authors propose a PSF scheduling for resolution enhancement.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) Equation 4: The authors can explicitly use a linear operator for PET system matrix as it is strictly defined by physical meaning. 2) I believe Eq. 6 is wrong. It should be system matrix transpose at the beginning. 3) PPCR is not clearly introduced. It is unclear to me how PSF is scheduled during the inference. The mechanism of its improvement on resolution is also unclear. 4) The implementation of CT cross-attention is unclear. This is important for the proposed method to leverage structural information from CT. 5) In the experiment, the details of the simulation are unclear. It is important for this work to have a specific application scenario where the low-resolution scanner that needs enhancement is clearly stated. Also, a 8-mm image domain PSF is too large for most modern scanners. 6) The real image-domain PSF is heterogeneous. This should be discussed in a study for resolution enhancement.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: Our method couples a CT-conditioned diffusion prior with scanner-aware PSF/DC sampling for PET SR. R1 considered it technically sound with standard/OOD and lesion-level gains; R2 noted CT guidance and PSF/PPCR improve quality in ablations; the meta-review appreciated the physics-constrained reconstruction. Q&A: 1.PSF/PPCR mechanism, CT attention, and reproducibility (Meta, R1.1-2, R3.3-4, R3.6). In DC, a candidate HR PET z is blurred by H and projected/rebinned by G_lr; the Poisson residual gives the likelihood gradient. The forward model is simplified but physics-informed, including PSF blur, projection/rebinning, and Poisson statistics, not simple image post-processing. PSF does not create resolution alone: diffusion proposes HR candidates, while PSF-aware DC keeps those whose degraded predictions match the measurement. Strong PSF constraints too early can over-restrict reverse diffusion before stable anatomy forms; PPCR therefore applies full physical constraints near the final high-fidelity stage. Table 3 shows removing DC, PSF, or PPCR degrades PSNR/SSIM/NMSE, supporting this mechanism. Since H is inference-time only, measured scanner PSFs, including spatially varying/heterogeneous PSFs with adjoints, can be used without retraining. CT cross-attention uses PET features as queries and multi-scale CT features as keys/values, outperforming CT concatenation in Table 3.To further support reproducibility, code and configurations will be released upon acceptance. 2.Simulation realism and application scenario (R1.3, R3.5-6). Real paired LR-HR PET is rarely available, while quantitative SR evaluation needs a reference; controlled simulation therefore enables metrics and fair comparison. Our LR generation is physics-based rather than plain downsampling: it includes PSF blur, projection geometry, angular/radial rebinning, Poisson statistics, and dose reduction. Thus 8/12 mm denote effective image-domain degradation settings for SRx4/OOD SRx6, not intrinsic detector resolution. The target application is resolution enhancement for legacy PET scanners with limited effective resolution: a high-quality PET/CT prior learned without LR-HR pairs can be combined with the available scanner operator/PSF to improve resolution and diagnostic utility. Standard/OOD gains and lesion-level SUV/NMSE gains support clinical fidelity. As this is a methodology paper, validation with measured scanner PSFs and fully 3D clinical pipelines is outside the scope of the current study. 3.ScorePET difference, hallucination, and runtime (Meta, R1.4, R2.1-2). ScorePET uses a PET score prior and PET likelihood/DC for reconstruction. In contrast, our work addresses PET SR under heterogeneous scanner-dependent LR observations with a different posterior formulation using CT conditioning, PSF-aware degradation, and PPCR-based physics-constrained sampling.Table 2 directly addresses R2’s comparison request: ours outperforms ScorePET in SRx4/OOD SRx6 on all metrics (PSNR +2.87/+2.81 dB). Hallucination is reduced because generated HR PET is constrained so that physically degraded outputs match measured LR PET and CT anatomy guides plausible structure; this is supported by Fig. 4 lesion SUV/NMSE and Table 3 consistency ablations. Runtime is 2.38 s, close to ScorePET/PETDM (2.08/1.96 s) and slower than single-pass UNet (0.004 s). With current computing power rapidly increasing, this moderate diffusion-level cost has translational value when it brings accuracy, lesion-fidelity, and robustness gains. 4.Notation/terminology (R1.5, R3.1-2). Eq. 4 defines ybar_lr(z)=G_lr H z+b_lr. By the chain rule, Eq. 6 applies the adjoint of the linear measurement operator G_lr H, i.e., H^T G_lr^T, to the Poisson residual, while b_lr is constant and does not affect the gradient. We will revise the notation to make this explicit, and define DC/abbreviations at first occurrence. These revisions do not affect implementation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposed a diffusion model-based method for PET super-resolution, utilizing CT as an anatomical prior in pre-training, and adding in physics constraints through PSF modeling. A mixture of review scores was received. The physics constraints in reconstruction was appreciated, but across the reviews more concerns arose, including clarifying PSF implementation details, its mechanism of improving resolution, and feasibility in implementing real image-domain PSF as it can be heterogeneous. These key questions might need to be sufficiently addressed during rebuttal, along with clarifying more implementation details as requested by R1 and R3.More discussion for results including hallucination reduction and computational cost might also be needed. | The authors have sufficiently addressed concerns raised in the previous round of revision, including physics awareness in diffusion process, forward model, and in data simulation. Generally the paper is interesting and the physics constraints in diffusion model are worth discussing in the community. The authors are encouraged to include more details of PSF schedule and simulation details as asked by R3 in their camera-ready version. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The three reviewers have recognized some novelty in the proposed PET superresolution method, which is based on a diffusion-based prior and physics-based sampling. The main limitations come from the 2D simulated slice-wise evaluation (R1) and model simplifications and clarity issues (R3). Despite these drawbacks, the framework seems interesting enough in its current state to spark discussion within the PET reconstruction community. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After rebuttal, the paper has two positive reviews (accept) and one remaining reject. The rebuttal reasonably addresses the main concerns from R1 and R2, particularly by clarifying the PSF-aware data consistency formulation, PPCR mechanism, distinction from ScorePET, likelihood-gradient notation, and planned code release. However, R3 remains unconvinced and continues to list several weaknesses: insufficient clarity in PSF scheduling, simulation realism, and reproducibility. Overall, I view the rebuttal as mostly successful: several concerns appear to be presentation/clarification issues rather than fundamental flaws. I would recommend acceptance, while noting that the final paper should improve clarity including the description of the PSF/PPCR implementation, CT cross-attention and simulation assumptions.

title: Kinetics-Informed Neural Representation for Dual-Tracer Dynamic PET Separation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The proposed method is technically interesting to the field. 2.The proposed method avoids the need for paired training data.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper relies heavily on visual comparisons and a few ROI parameter tables. There is a lac of tother quantitative metric, such as RMSE, SSIM comparison. 2.How do you evaluate the difference of the two injection’s time? Is 5 minutes enough? How about its generalizability? 3.My major question is related to Table I and II. In the FDG results, we could see much lower bias in Vb and K1, while others demonstrates a higher bias. In the MET results, we could see all the parameters other than vb all shows a higher bias. These results may partially reflect that the proposed method can not work well. Here is the reason: based on the basic kinetic modeling, please note that, K1 and Vb estimation’s sensitivity heavily depend on the early frames, as demonstrated in multiple papers. In other words, if you have 5 minutes time difference, you are be able to estimate an accurate K1 and Vb in the FDG case (this is the single-tracer), which is not related to the power of your proposed method. In the MET results, you have different ground truth for vb, which I think it is unreasonable from physiological perspective. Please clarify this clearer.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Novel INR-based formulation for dual-tracer PET: Uses an implicit neural representation to estimate voxel-wise kinetic parameters, introducing a spatially coherent alternative to noisy independent fitting. No need for single-tracer training data: Operates directly on dual-tracer dynamic images, improving practicality where ground truth single-tracer data is unavailable. Built-in regularization of kinetic estimation: The INR enforces spatial smoothness, addressing instability in voxel-wise kinetic modeling without explicit regularization. Demonstrated on real data: Inclusion of patient data supports clinical relevance beyond simulations.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The INR formulation is not clearly defined (e.g., patient- vs. tracer-specific). It appears to be patient- and tracer-pair specific, which may require per-scan optimization. However, training time and hardware requirements are not reported, making clinical feasibility difficult to assess. The paper does not describe how noise was modeled or added in the synthetic data. The chosen tracer pair (11C-MET + 18F-FDG) may represent a relatively easier separation scenario due to differences in half-life. Additionally, if the application targets brain tumors, the absence of a tumor in the synthetic data limits realism. Comparisons to standard analytical methods or alternative neural approaches are missing from several tables and figures, making it difficult to assess performance gains. Results lack error bars or statistical analysis, so significance cannot be evaluated. Unexplained hash encoding: Key parameters ((L, T, F, N_{\min}, b)) are introduced without explanation.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: -The authors use hash-encoding to model kinetic parameters effectively capturing details -Compartment models are integrated in the workflow ensuring a plausible relationship between tracer kinetics and tissue activity The combination of hash encoding and a lightweight MLP allows for fast training and inference, making it scalable for high-resolution PET data.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: In my opinion, the major weakness is that neural fields and MLPs are difficult to interpret. While the output (e.g., kinetic parameters) may be physiologically meaningful, understanding why the model predicts specific values for a given voxel can be challenging. Moreover, if the reconstructed images contain artefacts, it is very difficult to assess where the artefacts are coming from. Moreover, the authors compare their work only to one CNN working with 2D-slices (which is likely that it will not perform equally well) but do not compare their approach to other methods which might work equally well. Additionally, the description of the pipeline lacks details, making it impossible to reproduce the proposed approach. Therefore, while the approach is interesting, it lacks comparison to other works (e.g. https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/7/4089, https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6560/acc723).
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank R1, R2, R3 and Meta reviewer (M) for all insightful comments. Our responses are organised as below. 1.Method clarification. Our method targets the practical setting where only dual-tracer scans are obtained with paired single tracer images unavailable. Unlike deep learning methods relying on paired single data for training, we directly optimize each case to obtain separated signals from dual-tracer scans under kinetic constraints. 2.Quantitative evaluation (R1,R2,M). On real data, 3D metrics over nonzero frames show that, against DTS-INN, our method improves PSNR by 18.96/14.96 dB and SSIM by 0.684/0.628, and reduces NRMSE from 0.963/0.720 to 0.027/0.069 for FDG/AV45.Against LM, it improves PSNR by 6.31/10.83 dB and SSIM by 0.174/0.420, and reduces NRMSE from 0.061/0.268 to 0.027/0.069.For synthetic data, only dual-tracer measurements were simulated to match real acquisitions, so the GTs in Figs.2-3 are activity templates from noise-free TACs and our evaluation relies on TAC and visual comparison. We will add metric comparisons of TACs and report mean±std across synthetic cases. 3.K1&Vb concern (R1,M). We agree estimations of K1 & Vb depend strongly on early frames, but k2-k4 are highly coupled, so isolated biases do not necessarily indicate separation failure. If the gain came only from early-frame, LM should achieve comparable TACs under the same staggered information. But Fig. 5 shows that LM deviates at later frames while our method stays close to the reference, confirming the effectiveness of ours. For MET Vb, we agree that it should be consistent across tracers and will revise this in later simulations. 4.Injection interval (R1,R2). Injection interval trades off clinical feasibility and separation difficulty. Prior work (Pan, 2023) showed longer delays improve separability. Thus, we used 5 min for synthetic data as a challenging setting and 10 min for real data following the available protocol. Since our framework is case-specific and the input function includes injection timing, it can be extended to other intervals. 5.INR & Implementation (R2,R3,M). Our INR is scan and tracer pair specific, with the network optimized for each dual-tracer scan. As shown in Fig. 1, it does not synthesize images directly but maps voxel coordinates to tracer specific kinetic parameters. INR extends traditional voxel-wise curve fitting to image domain parameter estimation, improving spatial consistency over noise-sensitive fitting algorithms. Thus, interpretability comes from these constrained kinetic parameters rather than MLP. Hash encoding parameter definitions will be clarified in camera-ready. In L_Vb, Softplus ensures non-negativity and ReLU(Vb-1) penalizes Vb>1.Each synthetic case converges in 27.17 min on RTX 3060.6.Further baselines (R3). Direct comparison is limited by data, protocol, output form and code availability. Ref.1 requires paired single tracer data and outputs static images under a specific protocol, making fair comparison difficult. Ref.2 is based on spectral analysis and limited to image separation, so results mainly focus on TAC analysis. Under this setting, our method reduces NRMSE of compared TACs from 0.131/0.226 to 0.039/0.067 for FDG/AV45.7.Tracer pair/noise/tumor (R2). Although FDG and MET differ in half-life, the 5-min stagger still remains challenging. Our method is not limited to this tracer pair and can be extended to other combinations. Synthetic data were generated by Monte Carlo simulation (Lu,2023 & Sun,2023) with noise arising from the acquisition process. While current phantom was designed for controlled validation, we will add tumors in later simulations. 8.Case selection and figures (R2). The synthetic visual case was randomly selected, while the real data visualization used the only available case with same patient, dynamic brain PET of 2 tracers. Caption typos, table placement and Fig. 2/Fig. 3 overlap will be fixed, with DTS-INN TACs added in Fig. 5.Code will be released.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors introduced a kinetics-informed neural representation framework for dual-tracer separation. Instead of estimating kinetic parameters independently for each voxel, a neural network predicts tracer kinetic parameters from spatial coordinates through hash encoding and physiologically constrained kinetic parameter mapping through an MLP. Reviewers find the unsupervised, case-specific optimization technically interesting, and acknowledge its potential to improve spatial coherence in parameter maps. However, significant concerns are raised regarding INR formulation, the limited interpretability of neural fields and MLPs, the physiological validity of the results, and the limited generalization ability on pre-defined tracer pairs. R1 pointed out that the reported kinetic biases may indicate an inability to accurately separate the tracers beyond simple early-frame estimation. Also, the paper could benefit from improving its clarity and reproducibility since there are currently missing critical details including the MLP architecture, hash encoding parameters, and computational cost. The evaluation is currently mostly qualitative and could be insufficient in the aspect of quantitative metrics (e.g., RMSE, SSIM), missing statistical significance testing, and limited comparison against existing state-of-the-art analytical or neural separation methods. Thus, the authors are invited for rebuttal to address core concerns from the reviewers and clarify more details in the methodology. | Thank the authors for replying to all the reviewers. The merit of the work is acknowledged by most of the reviewers and most of the concerns are sufficiently addressed, except for (1) high bias in k2-k4 and (2) somewhat limited generalization ability to other tracer combinations since the INR is tracer specific, depending on the tracer kinetics. Weighing on all of these, I am leaning toward acceptance of the paper to initiate more discussion in the venue, but would not mind if a majority vote of rejection is given here. The authors are encouraged to further clarify the remaining concerns in addition to integrating edits in the rebuttal round to the manuscript. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): While two of the three reviewers opted for acceptance post-rebuttal, I cannot accept this paper as multiple important aspects are not explained and given the fact that no code is provided, I do not see how the method can be reproduced. Also, the novelty is not that high since to reference 24, and the evaluation is not sufficient to prove the method is an improvement beyond the state-of-the-art. Major problems: Reproducibility: The authors do not provide code nor promise to do so. This is in general not a problem, but under those circumstances, the requirements to the explanations are high. Sadly, the authors fail to explain multiple crucial aspects of the paper such as: a) how the arterial input function for each tracer is separated in the patient evaluation - this is not trivial, and key in the parameter estimation; not a word is spent on it. b) details on the MLP architecture (reviewer 3), the training process, the hash encoding (reviewer 2), and noise simulation in the synthetic data (reviewer 2) are not provided / sufficiently explained. Evaluation: Reviewer 1 already points out that the biases observed in the parameters hint that the tracers cannot be separated (see post-rebuttal justification of reviewer 1). Also, as reviewers 1, 2 and meta-reviewer 1 mention, the evaluation is mainly qualitative and the curves/images show practically no difference to the two proposed baselines. Numerical comparisons to the baselines are only partially provided in the rebuttal. More importantly, the baseline selection is suboptimal being the method of reference 24 open-source, and other relevant methods not discussed (see reviewer 3). Novelty: The authors claim that there INRs have never been used for dual-tracer kinetic parameter estimation. This is true, but the method proposed in reference 24 is extremely similar and its code is online. As a result, modifying the code to deal with two tracers is almost trivial in times of coding-optimized LLM. The reviewers actually praised the unsupervised character and the personalization with the “potential to improve spatial coherence in the parametric maps” as meta-reviewer 1 highlights, but that was already introduced in reference 24.Moreover, the strengths reviewers 1, 2 and partially 3 highlight are not new in the light of reference 24.Methodologically, the authors use hashing instead of Gaussian Fourier Features, which is a difference, but it is more of a design choice that likely does not impact the result massively. The use of a total variation regularization and a constraint on the range for Vb are standard choices, so also cannot be considered a contribution. In that sense, this paper is a small modification of reference 24 with new data. As a result, in my view, this is not sufficient novelty for MICCAI. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Although some reviewer concerns remain, I still find this work to have a strong clinical motivation and to be technically interesting

title: MAP-Diff: Multi-anchor Guided Diffusion for Progressive 3D Whole-Body Low-Dose PET Denoising
reviewer_1_strengths: By introducing clinically observed intermediate-dose anchors and timestep-dependent trajectory supervision, MAP-Diff constrains the reverse diffusion process to follow a dose-aligned and stage-consistent restoration path, addressing the mismatch between endpointonly objectives and progressive PET dose structure.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: It is suggested to include a discussion on the generalizability of the methods.
reviewer_1_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for the valuable feedback. We are encouraged that the reviewers recognized the effectiveness of the trajectory-level supervision design, particularly the timestep-dependent anchor guidance and dose-consistent denoising behavior of MAP-Diff. We address the main concerns below. Q1 (R2, Meta-R1): Gaussian diffusion vs. Poisson PET statistics. MAP-Diff does not require the diffusion forward process to be a physically exact model of PET photon-counting noise. Instead, the Gaussian forward process serves as a stochastic parameterisation of progressive image degradation. The key requirement is preservation of an ordered degradation structure across diffusion timesteps rather than exact equivalence between Gaussian and Poisson noise. Boundary calibration (Sec. 2.3) aligns diffusion states with real intermediate-dose PET images by matching degradation signatures (NMAE and SSIM within the body mask) relative to the clean full-dose image. Thus, the calibration targets statistically comparable degradation levels rather than identical noise distributions. Crucially, MAP-Diff supervises the clean prediction hat{x}_0(x_t,t) rather than the injected noise itself. Fig. 3 and Table 2 show that this trajectory-level supervision consistently improves both intermediate and final reconstruction quality over standard 3D DDPM using the same Gaussian diffusion formulation. Therefore, the observed gains arise from the proposed anchor-guided trajectory regularisation rather than the specific corruption model. Q2 (Meta-R1): Validity of trajectory alignment and whether it is interpolation. MAP-Diff is not an interpolation framework. The stochastic reverse diffusion process remains conditioned only on the 1/20-dose input, while anchors supervise only the predicted clean estimates during training and do not replace the reverse diffusion updates. The standard noise prediction objective (L_{noise}) also remains unchanged. If the model collapsed to deterministic interpolation, accurate noise pred across diffusion timesteps would be impossible. Instead, the anchor loss acts as a trajectory-level regulariser that guides clean predictions toward dose-consistent intermediate states while preserving stochastic generative behaviour. Table 2 further supports this interpretation: constant weighting (S8), which over-constrains all timesteps equally, significantly degrades performance compared with timestep-adaptive weighting. This indicates that MAP-Diff improves dose consistency through stage-wise trajectory regularisation rather than deterministic interpolation. Q3 (R1, Meta-R1): Generalizability and dependence on fixed anchors. MAP-Diff demonstrates cross-scanner generalisation on the external United Imaging uEXPLORER cohort under the clinically relevant 1/20-to-full-dose setting. The selected 1/10, 1/4, and 1/2 anchors are real intermediate-dose PET images available in the multi-dose dataset. Table 2 shows that one- or two-anchor variants still outperform the no-anchor baseline, indicating that MAP-Diff is not strictly dependent on any exact anchor combination, although full coverage provides the strongest guidance. Moreover, anchors are training-only; inference requires only the 1/20-dose input. MAP-Diff shows consistent improvements across both internal and external cohorts. Q4 (R1, R2, R3): Minor clarifications. The denoiser uses a 3D U-Net DDPM backbone. Timestep zones are calibrated rather than uniformly divided. The body mask is obtained by thresholding the non-background PET region. The loss weighting coefficient in Eq. (7) is fixed to lambda=0.2 across all experiments. MAP-Diff uses the same backbone and sampling procedure as 3D DDPM; anchors are training-only targets, so inference memory usage and runtime remain unchanged. We appreciate R2’s suggestions on additional diffusion baselines and 1/50-dose evaluation, which are complementary to the current study and do not affect the proposed trajectory-supervision formulation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors presented a multi-anchor guided diffusion framework to utilize intermediate-dose scans as anchors to supervise the reverse diffusion process and create a dose-aligned denoising path. All three reviewers acknowledged the novelty of the approach and its performance gain. However, several key concerns might still warrant a rebuttal. Statistical Modeling (Poisson vs. Gaussian). As pointed out by Reviewer 2, the paper models the Gaussian diffusion chain as a surrogate for PET’s inherent Poisson statistics. While this is a common approximation, it might be concerning at ultra-low dose levels (e.g., 1/20 or 1/50 dose) when the low photon count makes the Gaussian approximation significantly less accurate. Validity of the Trajectory Alignment. The Boundary Calibration was introduced to statistically align the intermediate diffusion outputs with intermediate dose levels. However, it remains unclear if this statistical alignment truly captures the physical dose characteristics or if it simply performs a sophisticated interpolation. Specifically, the mapping between the early trajectory and the starting dosage 1/10 might need a clearer physical justification. Generalizability and Fixed Anchors: Reviewer 1 and the AC are concerned that the denoising trajectory is overly dependent on the specific anchors (1/2, 1/4, 1/10) used during training, given the 1/20 dose as the conditioning. The cross-vendor evaluation was limited to the same 1/20 dose level, which might not sufficiently demonstrate the model’s generalization. The authors are encouraged to clarify these concerns along with other minor points given by the reviewers during the rebuttal phase. | The authors clarified that their trajectory does not model the exact physical model in low-dose imaging, but rather a stochastic parameterisation of progressive image degradation. This made the foundation of their work more solid. However, they didn’t further discuss the limitation in the generalization to different dose levels, especially when the conditioning has a different dose level rather than 1/20 dose, and for the ultra low dose 1/50 level pointed out by R2. A remaining concern of mine is whether the denoising trajectory modeling in training is limited to a specific low dose input and for all other intermediate dose levels. Considering these, I am giving a weak acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers are positive about this paper. After reviewing the feedback from both the reviewers and the authors, I believe the paper meets the acceptance criteria and recommend acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors have addressed the reviewers questions.

title: MetaVFM: Meta-Learned Efficient Adaptation of Vision Foundation Models for Medical Imaging
reviewer_1_strengths: 1- The problem is well-motivated with clear empirical justification. Figure 1 demonstrates that LoRA performance varies non-monotonically across module-rank combinations and that optimal configurations differ across datasets. 2- The design of the Super-Adapter is technically elegant. The nested prefix parametrization where lower-rank adapters prefixes of higher ones and share a common core is an interesting idea. Training a single super adapter per dataset to generate an entire adapter zoo is significantly more efficient than training independent adapters for each config. 3- The retrieval-based inference mechanism eliminates the need for any hyperparameter search on new datasets — a single cosine similarity lookup replaces multiple training runs. 4- Evaluating on 17 datasets spanning fine-grained, general, scene, and medical domains provides broad coverage. The fact that all evaluation datasets are held out from meta-space training makes the retrieval genuinely zero-shot and the evaluation honest.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Accuracy gains over the methods in Table 1 at 100 epochs is marginal. Table 1 shows MetaVFM achieves only 0.2 points average improvement over APLA. It is also unclear whether the difference between the other methods is significant, e. g. , 91.0 AdaptFormer vs 91.9 MetaVFM. Without statistical significance testing or standard deviations reported in Table 1, this difference is essentially within noise range and cannot be considered a meaningful accuracy improvement over the strongest parameter selection methods. 2.Table 2 only compares convergence speed against basic methods — Linear Probing, MLP, Full Fine-tuning, and LoRA. The strongest methods from Table 1 — APLA, ARC, GPS, SPT-Adapter — are entirely absent from the convergence analysis. Since these methods also use sophisticated initialization and configuration selection strategies, they may converge just as quickly as MetaVFM. Without this comparison the 2–3× faster convergence claim is only demonstrated against weak baselines and cannot be generalized to the full set of competitors. 3.The meta-space is trained on 90+ datasets but the paper never lists which datasets were used. Without this information it is impossible to verify whether the evaluation datasets represent genuinely novel visual types or whether similar dataset types — for example other bird classification or retinal imaging datasets — were present during training. This is a fundamental evaluation transparency issue that undermines the “truly unseen” claim. 4.Training one Super-Adapter per dataset across 90+ datasets is the most computationally expensive part of the framework, yet the paper never reports the total wall-clock time, GPU hours, or computational cost of building the adapter zoo. Without this the practical feasibility of the approach for other researchers is unclear, and the claimed efficiency advantage over per-task search is only partially substantiated. 5.In the ablation results presented in Table 3, mean +- std results show significant overlap between different components of the method. It is unclear whether these results are statistically significant.

reviewer_3_strengths: Computational Efficiency via Meta-knowledge: The transition from iterative per-task searching to a predictive meta-learning paradigm is highly significant. By bypassing the traditional training step budget overhead, the work addresses a major practical bottleneck in applying foundation models to diverse medical imaging modalities. Extensive Empirical Validation: The authors demonstrate the robustness of their approach by evaluating MetaVFM across 17 distinct datasets. The reported 2-3x speedup in convergence while maintaining or exceeding the accuracy of established PEFT methods like LoRA and AdaptFormer provides a compelling case for the utility of the Meta-Adapter Space.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: W1: Ambiguity in Meta-Feature Extraction for Medical Tasks. A critical technical omission is the detailed explanation of how the system extracts “meta-features” from a previously unseen medical dataset to query the Meta-Adapter Space. If the meta-features rely on generic ImageNet-based descriptors, the framework might struggle with highly specialized medical textures (e.g., OCT or histopathology) that differ fundamentally from natural images. A formal analysis or visualization of the meta-space distribution for medical vs. non-medical tasks is necessary. W2: Over-reliance on Super-Adapter Convergence Stability. The entire framework hinges on the quality of the Super-Adapter. However, the paper lacks a theoretical or empirical proof regarding the stability of training a single shared-weight structure on over 90 heterogeneous datasets. There is a risk of “inter-task interference” where the weights favor dominant natural image features over subtle medical ones, yet the authors do not provide an ablation study on how the composition of the meta-training set influences downstream medical performance. W3: Lack of Domain-Specific Baseline Comparisons. While the paper compares MetaVFM against general-purpose PEFT methods, it fails to include recent medical-specific adaptation techniques, such as those incorporating clinical knowledge graphs or domain-specific self-supervised pre-training. Comparing MetaVFM against a foundation model already pre-trained on medical data (e.g., RadImageNet) would clarify if the meta-learning gains are complementary to domain-specific pre-training. W4: Missing Structural Sensitivity Analysis. The manuscript asserts that MetaVFM predicts the best “rank” and “location” for adapters. However, there is no visualization or table showing what these predicted configurations actually look like for medical tasks compared to natural ones. For instance, do medical tasks consistently require deeper adapter placement or higher rank allocation? Providing these insights would validate the “intelligence” of the meta-learner beyond simple accuracy metrics. W5: Implementation Complexity and Reproducibility Concerns. The complexity of the Meta-Adapter Space and the dual-stage training process (Super-Adapter training followed by Meta-learner optimization) presents a high barrier for clinical researchers. Without more granular details on the hyper-network architecture or the specific loss functions used to align the meta-space, reproducing the results on private clinical datasets remains a significant challenge. w6.Lack of latest paper citations. author_feedback: We thank R1, R3, and R5 for their feedback. We are encouraged that they recognized MetaVFM’s strengths: R1 highlighted the motivation, Super-Adapter design, zero-shot retrieval, and held-out evaluation; R3 found the method novel/inspiring and experiments comprehensive; and R5 recognized the value of replacing per-task search with predictive meta-learning. We clarify the concerns below. [R1] Accuracy gains. The key result in Tab.1 is consistency: MetaVFM remains top-1/2 across heterogeneous datasets, while others perform well on some datasets but drop on others. This matters because the target dataset is unknown in advance. A paired Wilcoxon test gives: MetaVFM-T5 vs. APLA: 11 wins/2 ties/4 losses, p≈0.035, and vs. AdaptFormer: 16 wins/1 loss, p≈0.0016.Tab 1 std± were omitted due to space and will be added on GitHub. MetaVFM jointly selects rank, placement, and initialization without per-task search, using <3M trainable params vs. ~7M for APLA. Thus, the contribution is an accuracy, convergence-speed, and parameter-efficiency trade-off, not only an accuracy gain. [R1, R5] Zoo transparency, cost, and reproducibility. The 91-dataset catalog can’t fit in the paper, and MICCAI disallows textual/PDF supplementary. We will release the full catalog on GitHub and add the held-out protocol in the paper to verify the “unseen” setting. Zoo construction is a one-time offline cost: it took only 5 days on 8 GPUs for all 91 datasets (~2 GPU-hours per dataset-backbone). Compared with per-task search, a single adapter costs ~1 GPU-hour, so heuristic search over a few rank/placement candidates already exceeds the Super-Adapter cost. Meta-space training takes ~1h on an M3 laptop. For a new dataset, MetaVFM only needs millisecond retrieval + short fine-tuning, not zoo rebuilding. The repo will include scripts, configs, checkpoints, and embeddings. [R1] Convergence and ablation. Tab.2 targets MetaVFM’s specific claim: reducing steps-to-accuracy via dataset-aware initialization. APLA/ARC/GPS/SPT-Adapter are strong structure/search baselines, but do not provide such initialization nor claim faster convergence. Tab.3 further supports this claim: it evaluates the full 1/5/10-epoch trajectory, not only epoch-10 overlap. Removing meta-initialization drops epoch-1 average by 4.8%, showing that the learned initialization drives faster early adaptation. Rank/FID/PCA losses mainly refine retrieval geometry, so their gains are smaller but consistent. [R5] Medical Meta-features. Dataset embeddings are computed from sampled images using self-supervised DINO features with PCA/FID geometry, not ImageNet classifier outputs. The meta-space visualization (Fig.3) supports this: medical datasets occupy nearby regions, suggesting meaningful medical-domain structure rather than generic natural-image semantics. [R3] Other PEFTs. R3’s suggestion is insightful. We use LoRA because rank/placement gives a flexible parameter–performance trade-off, but the current space inherits LoRA’s limits. Extending the zoo to other PEFTs is a promising direction to select the best adapter family per dataset. [R5] Super-Adapter. We do not train one Super-Adapter across all 90+ datasets. Each dataset–backbone pair has its own Super-Adapter, sharing weights only across ranks/placements within that dataset and not across tasks. Task transfer occurs later through the meta-space. [R5] Structural sensitivity and citations. We agree this is a useful interpretability analysis. We, indeed, did it and found that active sites vary across datasets, from sparse layouts (few layers are adapted) to dense ones. We also observe domain-specific trends: medical tasks often favor attention-heavy placements, while texture datasets use lighter, low-rank patterns. Due to space, we omitted it, but we will release the meta-space/zoo for further study of rank allocation and structure/accuracy trade-offs. We will cite the most relevant suggested works and clarify how they differ from ours in objectives.

(3) Describe the pre-training dataset zoo, and clarify whether medical tasks are included and how test-data leakage is prevented. | After rebuttal, the paper received positive scores, with 1 “Reject” shifting to “Accept”. Reviewers originally recommending “Accept” remained positive. The clarifications provided by the authors are convincing. I endorse acceptance and expect the authors to incorporate the promised additional dataset details in the project’s repository. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The manuscript is recommended for acceptance as the post-rebuttal consensus shifted positively, with reviewers commending the technical novelty of the meta-learned adapter space and the efficiency of the Super-Adapter design. Nevertheless, the decision notes significant reservations raised during the discussion phase regarding the marginal practical effect size, borderline statistical significance, and potential test-data leakage from the undisclosed meta-training zoo. The authors are strictly required to fulfill their rebuttal commitments—specifically integrating the full 91-dataset catalog, reporting all standard deviations, and providing the structural sensitivity analysis—in the final camera-ready version to guarantee transparency and reproducibility. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an important and practical problem in adapting Vision Foundation Models without expensive per-task hyperparameter search. Reviewers generally agreed that the motivation is strong, the proposed meta-adapter framework is technically interesting, and the evaluation across diverse unseen datasets is comprehensive. The rebuttal also addressed several major concerns regarding dataset transparency and additional analysis. While some performance gains are modest in the fully converged setting, the practical benefit of reducing search cost and improving convergence efficiency was considered valuable. Overall, the paper provides a meaningful contribution and I support acceptance.

title: Multi-depth Rubidium PET Graph Neural Network for Major Adverse Cardiac Event Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) Positive results: the results validate the authors’ assumptions that: (a) tracking the perfusion at multiple depths is better than at a single depth; (b) graph neural network is more fitted for the geometrical nature of the task. 2) Details for reproduction: the authors provide a lot of details about their method and experiments, which can be assumed to facilitate reproduction. 3) Possible clinical impact: although this study was retrospective, any improvement in cardiovascular risk prediction has a chance to benefit the patients.
