reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Area Chair and reviewers for their constructive comments and positive evaluation. Below, we briefly clarify the main concerns and outline future directions. 1.Practical relevance and clinical scalability (R1, R3): The reviewers raised concerns about the controlled setting and clinical scalability. We clarify that TOF-GR was evaluated on both BrainWeb low-count simulation data with small lesions and real clinical TOF-PET/CT data, demonstrating feasibility in quantitative and clinical scenarios. The 128×128×96 preprocessing/cropping was used to satisfy 3D memory constraints and ensure fair comparison with MLEM, DIP, and INR. Full-resolution, whole-body, and larger-scale clinical validation will be studied in future work. 2.Computational cost and scalability (R2, R3): The reviewers noted the need for computational analysis. This work focuses on establishing TOF-GR as a new explicit representation rather than fully optimizing runtime. Compared with INR’s global coordinate-to-intensity MLP, TOF-GR uses local anisotropic Gaussian primitives, reducing the burden of global implicit fitting. Our implementation runs on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU and shows lower cost than INR under the same setting. Systematic runtime and memory benchmarking will be future work. 3.OSEM initialization and hyperparameter sensitivity (R1, R2, R3): OSEM is only used to initialize Gaussian positions and intensities; the final reconstruction is optimized by the Gaussian representation, TOF-aware forward model, Poisson likelihood, TV penalty, and anatomical kernel prior. Table 2 shows that the kernel prior improves stability across different k and λ settings. Robustness to poorer OSEM initialization, especially in extremely low-count cases, will be further investigated. 4.Baseline comparison and ablation (R1, R2, R3): All baselines were evaluated under the same data setting and resolution. MLEM, DIP, and INR represent classical iterative, unsupervised CNN-based, and coordinate-based implicit reconstruction methods. The current ablation focuses on the kernel prior and key parameters, directly supporting the claims of anatomical regularization and improved stability. More analyses on Gaussian primitives, covariance parameterization, TOF modeling, and TV regularization will be future work. 5.Clarity, visualization, reproducibility, and ethics (R1, R2, R3): The MRI/CT-guided kernel prior does not transfer anatomical intensity into PET; it regularizes the Gaussian tracer distribution within a plausible anatomical manifold. Clinical PET/CT data were retrospectively collected and anonymized, without intervention or identifiable patient information. We also agree that vectorized/high-resolution figures, code release, and more implementation details are valuable and will further address them in future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a Gaussian Splatting (GS) representation when solving for a low-count PET reconstruction, moving away from discrete grids while favoring interpretability over implicit representations. The method includes a TOF forward model (system matrix, Poisson likelihood) and a kernel-based anatomical prior. The three reviewers acknowledge that the use of GS in the context of PET imaging is novel. Reviewers have highlighted consistent improvements achieved by the proposed method over several baselines (MLEM, DIP, INR) and across brain and thorax datasets, although the ablation study was considered limited. Some issues were raised regarding the lack of discussion of scalability to full-resolution images and in clinical context, computational complexity, dependence on OSEM in the low-count setting, and sensitivity to hyperparameters. These should be discussed in the revised paper. Section 2.2., and the experimental setting (including the number of patients) need clarification. Include vectorized images for the results. Also, provide the code or enough details to guarantee reproducibility.

title: Tracer-Adaptive Expert Learning for Generalizable PET Lesion Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Moving away from standard feature-driven MoE gating to a biologically grounded, prototype-driven routing mechanism is relatively innovative. 2.The evaluation on 1,366 scans across three diverse tracers is comprehensive. The zero-shot generalization testing on a completely unseen tracer (CD70) proves the model’s scalability.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Cascading Error Vulnerability: The routing logic strictly depends on anatomical occupancy maps generated by a frozen CT backbone pre-trained on TotalSegmentator. If the CT segmentation fails due to poor contrast, metal artifacts, or unusual patient positioning, the physiological expectation embedding will be flawed, causing the MoE routing to collapse. The paper lacks an ablation study analyzing the framework’s robustness to anatomical segmentation errors. 2.Scalability Bottleneck: The ablation study reveals that increasing the number of experts to K=36 degrades overall performance. The authors hypothesize that excessive sparsity hinders shared representation learning. For a foundation-level architecture aiming to handle an expanding array of tracers, this capacity limit must be addressed or mathematically bounded.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) The paper addresses a clinically important and technically challenging problem. Multi-tracer PET lesion segmentation is genuinely difficult because lesions and physiological uptake often share similar high-intensity appearances, and correct interpretation inherently depends on both anatomical location and tracer type. The problem formulation is well-scoped and the clinical motivation is clearly articulated throughout. (2) The core motivation is well-grounded and matches clinical reasoning. Guiding expert routing with anatomical context and tracer-specific physiological priors is a more principled approach than standard feature-only MoE gating, and the design mirrors how nuclear medicine physicians interpret PET studies in practice. The “conflicting gradient” problem identified in conventional MoE under multi-tracer settings is a genuine and underappreciated failure mode that this work directly addresses. (3) The method has meaningful novelty at the application level. The combination of PE2 embedding, prototype-driven routing with a joint anatomical-physiological similarity metric, and dual-stage feature modulation is a thoughtful and coherent formulation. The use of an LLM to curate a multi-tracer physiological atlas as structured prior knowledge is an interesting design choice, and the K-Medoids initialization strategy for expert prototypes reflects careful attention to training stability. (4) The experimental results are compelling, particularly in terms of parameter efficiency. ProMoE achieves state-of-the-art performance with only 6M parameters, approximately 1.5% of nnU-Net, while outperforming all multi-tracer baselines by a substantial margin, especially in the PSMA domain (+8.93% DSC over SwinUNETR). The result that ProMoE surpasses single-tracer specialists in the data-scarce FAPI setting further supports the value of the proposed cross-tracer knowledge sharing mechanism.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) The “zero-shot generalization” claim requires more careful qualification. The paper claims zero-shot generalization to the unseen CD70 tracer, which is partially accurate in that no CD70 training data is used. However, the method relies on tracer-specific physiological priors for CD70 at test time, encoded in the PE2 embedding. This makes the setting more precisely described as prior-guided zero-shot rather than strictly blind zero-shot generalization. The authors should clarify how the CD70 physiological prior was constructed and whether any CD70 uptake characteristics were known a priori, as this directly affects the validity of the zero-shot claim. (2) The contribution of the routing mechanism itself is not fully isolated from the backbone advantage. ProMoE uses a frozen CT backbone pre-trained on TotalSegmentator, providing structured anatomical supervision not available to the baselines. While all methods receive PET+CT as input, the quality of anatomical conditioning differs substantially, making it difficult to attribute performance gains specifically to the proposed prototype-driven routing. A controlled baseline sharing the same frozen CT backbone but using standard feature-driven routing would more cleanly isolate the routing contribution. The ablation in Table 2 partially addresses this within the ProMoE family, but does not resolve the fairness concern against external baselines. (3) Several technical details are insufficiently specified. The binarization threshold in 1(v), the motivation for squaring S_Phy in the joint similarity score, the selection criterion for the hard threshold theta, and whether K=12 was chosen via cross-validation are all left unspecified. The squaring of S_Phy in particular is a non-trivial design decision that warrants either theoretical justification or an ablation. These gaps modestly limit reproducibility and confidence in the formulation. (4) The generalization claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence supports. The unseen-tracer test set contains only 30 CD70 cases, which is a small sample for drawing strong conclusions about zero-shot generalization. Center-disjoint evaluation is also absent, making it difficult to fully assess cross-domain robustness. The generalization claims in the abstract and conclusion should be toned down to better reflect the scope of the current evidence.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Atlas-based encoding of anatomical uptake expectations enables context-aware interpretation, and the method shows strong robustness in physiologically confounded regimes (e.g. PSMA, FAPI), addressing a key limitation of existing approaches.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The paper’s core claim of improved physiological–pathological disambiguation in multi-tracer setup necessitates evaluation of organ-wise false positive rates and region-specific error breakdowns. The current reliance on aggregate DSC and NSD, while standard, leaves the link between the proposed mechanism and the reported improvements largely implicit, particularly for FDG, where gains are marginal. The qualitative examples in Fig. 3 are illustrative but limited in scope, and do not fully substantiate the claimed behaviour across the dataset. The ablation in Table 2 suggests that the MoE routing contributes unevenly across tracers. For FDG, the FiLM-conditioned baseline (K=1) performs within ~2% DSC/NSD of the full ProMoE, indicating that atlas-based conditioning alone nearly saturates performance for metabolically diffuse tracers. The more substantial gains on PSMA and FAPI are encouraging, but it would strengthen the paper to clarify whether these stem from the prototype-driven routing specifically or from the increased model capacity that additional experts provide. An experiment comparing a single-branch architecture with tracer-conditional FiLM parameters against the full ProMoE at matched parameter count would help disentangle these factors. Reliability of generated uptake priors, and uncertainty from LLM based physiological uptake atlas impacts the reproducibility and robustness, and would benefit from validation.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: 1.Claim calibration (R2, R3) We agree that several claims should be stated more precisely. In the revision, we will replace “physiological-pathological disentanglement” with “physiological-context-aware segmentation” and “zero-shot generalization” with “prior-guided zero-shot transfer.” We will also explicitly state the limited CD70 cohort size and the lack of center-disjoint evaluation as limitations, with broader validation left for future work. Thus, the submitted evidence supports improved context-aware multi-tracer segmentation, rather than unrestricted foundation-level generalization. 2.CT segmentation dependence and fairness (R1, R2) While relying on CT segmentation is a limitation we will note in the revision, ProMoE is architecturally designed for robustness against segmentation: (1) PE2 utilizes coarse patch-level organ occupancy rather than precise boundaries; (2) multiple experts whose joint similarities exceed a threshold are activated during training. This redundancy ensures that each expert is exposed to sufficiently diverse scenarios, thereby improving robustness to imperfect CT segmentation. Regarding comparison fairness, FiLM w/o MoE in Table 2 incorporates frozen CT backbone but excludes the MoE architecture. Its performance is inferior to external baselines such as nnUNet and SwinU, indicating that ProMoE’s gains do not stem from anatomical conditioning. Furthermore, under the K=12 setting, MLP-MoE performs worse than ProMoE, suggesting the improvements are not simply due to larger model capacity. 3.CD70 evaluation (R2, R3) For CD70, no images, labels, or results were used in the training stage. Only a fixed CD70 physiological prior, curated before evaluation (see response 4), was used at inference. We therefore redefine this as prior-guided zero-shot transfer. Its clinical significance lies in the fact that obtaining physiological distributions of new tracers is far more feasible than acquiring dense annotations. As R3 noted, this transferability assumes partial overlap between CD70 and seen tracers in normal uptake patterns. Fully new local uptake patterns may require extending the prototype space, which we will add as a limitation and future direction. 4.Reproducibility and atlas construction (R2, R3) Upon acceptance, we will release the code, configs, uptake atlas, and documentation needed to reproduce the reported models. The indicator 1(.) denotes non-zero support. S_Phy is non-negative, we empirically square it to emphasize stronger physiological consistency. We set θ = 1/K so that the sparsity threshold adapts to expert granularity. K=12 was selected by cross-validation on seen tracers. The atlas was LLM-drafted and then reviewed by two senior nuclear medicine experts. It is used as a fixed deterministic lookup table, so LLM randomness does not affect training or reproducibility. 5.Clinical aspects and why MoE (R3) We attempted to fuse encoded PET physiological text with image features using non-MoE architectures, but observed no performance gain. This is mainly because existing medical text encoders produce highly similar embeddings for structurally similar PET physiological pattern descriptions and cannot effectively resolve cross-tracer gradient conflicts discussed in Introduction. In contrast, ProMoE routes physiologically conflicting patches by expert prototypes to distinct experts, structurally alleviating this issue. Moreover, FDG dominates the absolute sample size in our dataset, its broader feature distribution fundamentally anchors the shared parameter space. Even with balanced batch sampling, single-branch models inevitably bias toward FDG-dominant patterns and fail on less frequent, more complex tracers. The results validate this: models w/o MoE fail on highly confounded tracers, whereas ProMoE achieves its most substantial gains on PSMA/FAPI. Conversely, baselines are already well-optimized for the dominant FDG distribution, explaining the marginal gains there.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The manuscript proposes a nice approach to segment lesions in PET/CT guided by anatomical and physiological knowledge inspired in the expert approach. The technical implementation is also parameter-effective while providing marginal advantages to the compared baselines. Yet, important aspects need to be explained in a rebuttal and modified in case the paper gets accepted. In particular, the claims made should be adapted to the obtained results (reviewer 2, criticism 4, reviewer 3, first paragraph of weaknesses), the dependance on CT segmentation should be discussed (reviewer 1, criticism 1 and reviewer 2, criticism 2), details should be given for the CD7 evaluation (reviewer 2, criticism 1, reviewer 3, optional comments), relevant aspects for reproducibility should be addressed (reviewer 2, criticism 3, reviewer 3, second paragraph of weaknesses), and clinical aspects of uptake patterns (reviewer 3) should be commented. Additionally, it is requested for the authors to make a statement if the code will be made available, as without it reproducibility is not really granted. | In view of the post-rebuttal evaluation of the reviewers, I follow their recommendation and recommend approval. Still, I remain critical on the claims as I was on the first iteration and strongly encourage the authors to consider the post-rebuttal comments of reviewer 3.While I do not have means to enforce this, I hope the authors do not ignore the comment and include this in the limitation section. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): the rebuttal convinced the reviewers and they all agree for acceptance. A successful rebuttal period with addressing the majority of concerns. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors proposed ProMoE, a prototype-driven Mixture-of-Experts framework with anatomical and physiological priors to integrate clinical reasoning into multi-tracer PET lesion segmentation. The major concerns from the previous round were properly addressed, including the CT segmentation dependence (patch level robustness is shown in Fig 3), details on the generalization test on an unseen dataset (CD70), and fairness and clinical aspects in MoE selection. My recommendation would also be acceptance.

title: TracerAD: Training-Free Few-Shot 3D Anomaly Detection for Novel PET Tracers
reviewer_1_strengths: First, the problem setting is highly clinically relevant. The paper directly targets a realistic PET deployment scenario in which only a few healthy references exist and no patient labels are yet available, which is more practical than standard large-cohort supervised training. Second, the method is well aligned with clinical intuition. SAFD captures fine focal deviations, RCSM adds robustness to within-ROI variation and registration imprecision, and TAMR models circuit-level metabolic disruption, making the framework more compelling than a single-scale retrieval scheme. Third, the reported empirical results are promising. At 10-shot, TracerAD reaches 84.13% AUC, 78.83% weighted F1, and 81.60% sensitivity, outperforming the supervised baseline in most settings, and it achieves 86.60% sensitivity at 2-shot. The voxel-wise 3D heatmaps are also a meaningful strength because they add anatomical interpretability beyond subject-level labels. Fourth, the ablation study is reasonably informative. The paper shows additive gains from SAFD to RCSM to TAMR and suggests that sparse graph reasoning improves both performance and stability.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The biggest weakness is that the algorithmic novelty is somewhat narrower than the framing suggests. SAFD is closely related to patch-matching and retrieval-based anomaly detection ideas such as Roth et al. ’s Towards Total Recall in Industrial AD (CVPR 2022) and RAD (Long et al. , 2026), while RCSM and TAMR are explicitly close in spirit to UniVAD’s component-aware matching and graph-based interaction module (Gu et al. , CVPR 2025). In that sense, the paper’s novelty lies more in problem formulation and PET-specific integration than in a fundamentally new core formulation. Second, the comparison is limited. The main baseline is a supervised few-shot classifier from Liu et al. , so it remains unclear how TracerAD compares against stronger unsupervised or training-free anomaly detection baselines that are methodologically closer to the proposed approach, especially retrieval/matching-based ones such as UniVAD or RAD. Third, The 3D heatmaps are compelling qualitatively, but there is no voxel-/region-level ground-truth evaluation or reader study to establish localization validity. Fourth, the framework relies heavily on registration and atlas quality. Small misregistrations may affect SAFD and RCSM substantially, yet no robustness analysis is provided. The equal-weight fusion is also reasonable but somewhat heuristic.

author_feedback: Thanks for the valuable comments. We appreciate the recognition of our work’s clinical relevance and have addressed each concern as follows. 1.Method design and positioning (R1): We acknowledge the intellectual lineage from retrieval-based anomaly detection. TracerAD is not a direct adaptation but a domain-specific redesign for 3D brain PET. Existing methods such as UniVAD rely on component segmentation modules designed for industrial images, where each image contains a small number of distinct objects. Brain PET volumes, by contrast, encompass over a hundred fine-grained anatomical regions with continuous metabolic gradients, making learnable component segmentation inappropriate. TracerAD instead leverages the AAL3 atlas, a widely adopted neuroanatomical parcellation, to define matching regions directly. Similarly, SAFD exploits the coordinate-level alignment provided by MNI152 registration, which is more precise than the local neighborhood matching used in 2D retrieval methods. To our knowledge, TracerAD is the first training-free few-shot framework for 3D brain anomaly detection. 2.Baseline comparison (R1): The supervised baseline from Liu et al. uses the same DINO backbones, providing a fair comparison under a consistent feature extraction pipeline. The key finding is that TracerAD, under a stricter unsupervised protocol using only N unlabeled HCs, matches or exceeds a supervised method requiring 2N labeled samples. Existing training-free methods such as UniVAD and RAD operate on 2D natural images and are not directly applicable to 3D brain PET without substantial redesign. 3.Heatmap localization evaluation (R1, R2): Unlike tumors with well-defined boundaries, PET tracer deposition in neurodegenerative diseases is diffuse and spatially heterogeneous, and no pixel-level ground-truth annotations exist for such patterns. In clinical practice, nuclear medicine physicians describe regional uptake qualitatively rather than delineating precise lesion boundaries, even for established tracers. For novel tracers, this challenge is further compounded by the absence of known deposition patterns. Voxel-level localization metrics such as Dice score are therefore inapplicable, and subject-level classification metrics remain the standard evaluation protocol in PET anomaly detection. We note that the group-average heatmaps in Fig. 2 show patterns consistent with known amyloid deposition, providing preliminary evidence of localization validity. Individual case visualization will be provided in the journal extension due to the conference page limit. 4.Registration robustness (R1): MNI152 registration and AAL3 parcellation are the standard pipeline in neuroimaging research. The RCSM branch addresses registration imprecision through region-level average pooling before matching, absorbing minor spatial shifts within each atlas region. We will explore personalized atlas segmentation and registration-free variants in the journal extension. 5.Implementation details and inference time (R3): We will release the source code upon acceptance to ensure full reproducibility. Unlike routine disease screening, our cold-start scenario prioritizes diagnostic accuracy over inference speed, as manually interpreting scans from unfamiliar tracers is extremely challenging. 6.Backbone and application scope (R3): We selected the DINO family because DINOv3 produces brain-like activation patterns aligned with neuroanatomical structures. The four-backbone comparison demonstrates robustness to backbone choice. TracerAD has also been applied to a novel tracer currently undergoing regulatory review, though results cannot be disclosed at this time due to ongoing approval processes. The ADNI evaluation presented in this paper demonstrates the method’s feasibility on a publicly available dataset. We will explore 3D medical backbones and additional tracers in the journal extension.
